_comment: Contribution 1: how a subject is turned into a skill tree. This was spec/decomposition.md until 0.3.0, and is now a prompt module like the other four, so that all five contributions have the same shape and the same kind of version. It is NOT composed into anything a student sees -- `audience` says who it is for, and the engine skips it when it loads the instructions for a tree. prompts/authoring.json wraps it for a teacher.
title: The decomposition model

sections.about: This specification turns a curriculum, or a teacher's topic list, into a skill tree. The output is one file, `tree.csv`, plus a short subject note. The engine draws everything from that file, so a subject is authored by writing learning outcomes and their dependencies, never by arranging boxes. The schema and rules are the same in every language. Rules for one family of subjects are in the family blocks at the end (`subjectFamilies`).
sections.whatIsANode:
Every node has a **type**. A **concept** is declarative knowledge: a definition, a named quantity, a rule stated in words. A **skill** is a procedure or higher-order capability: what the student does.

**When a concept needs extensive work before a student could be said to have practised it, that work is a separate skill node** that lists the concept as a prerequisite. The concept node tests understanding (explain it, judge a borderline case, tell it from a look-alike); the skill node trains execution. The type also decides the form of the description (`descriptionForm`).

The name shows the type:

- a **concept** takes a **noun phrase**, the concept itself: "Power", not "The concept of a power";
- a **skill** takes a **verb phrase** for what the student does: "Draw a table and a graph for a function".

A skill named with a noun, or a concept named with a verb, needs reconsidering. Which verbs to use depends on the family (`skillVerbs` in its block).
sections.descriptionForm:
The `description` cell holds **only what the node requires**. The engine prints the lead-in in front of it, “The student can:” for a skill and “The student can explain:” for a concept, so never write a lead-in into the cell.

### A skill is a bare verb phrase

Start with the verb, with no subject; the cell continues the lead-in:

- `add two multi-digit numbers, including cases that carry`
- `decide whether two fractions are equal, and write a fraction in a different but equal form`

Not `The student can add …`, and not `Adding …`. **One `can` per node**: `solve …, and knows why the method works` breaks under the lead-in. Write `solve …, and explain why the method works`, or, usually better, split it into two nodes.

### A concept is written `Term: definition`

Always, one line per concept, even when the node has one concept and the term is its name. The definition is written as a definition, not as a sentence about the student:

```csv
metallic-bond,concept,Bonding,Metallic bond,"Metallic bond: the attraction between positive metal ions and a sea of free valence electrons surrounding them.",,,
```

Not `The student knows that a metallic bond is …`, and not `A metallic bond is …`.

### A node may define several concepts

For concepts that only exist as a pair (`Intron and exon`), write one line per definition, with a real line break inside the quoted cell:

```csv
intron-exon,concept,Gene expression,Intron and exon,"Intron: a non-coding stretch that is cut out of the pre-mRNA.
Exon: a coding stretch that is kept.",transcription,,
```

Only what stands before the FIRST colon on a line is the term, so a definition may contain colons. Keep this to concepts genuinely learned together; unrelated definitions are separate nodes.

### A difference between two concepts is a skill

`knows the difference between X and Y` does not belong in a concept node. Define both concepts, one line each; where the contrast itself will be tested, add a skill node `Explain the difference between X and Y` that depends on the concept node.
sections.dataModel:
One row per node in `tree.csv`. The schema is the same in every language; only the values are in the subject's language.

| Column | Type | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| `id` | text, unique | Short, URL-friendly identifier, kebab-case. Used as a foreign key elsewhere. E.g. `percentage-growth-factor` |
| `type` | `skill` \| `concept` | See `whatIsANode`. **The value is an English data enum in every language**, including in a Norwegian or Swedish file. Only the displayed label is translated. |
| `topic` | text | Subject area used for visual grouping, e.g. "Statistics". Decides which column the node is drawn in. Purely visual — it does not affect dependencies. An empty value lands in a catch-all column with a console warning. |
| `name` | text | Short display name in the box. See the naming convention in `whatIsANode`. |
| `description` | text | What the node requires, and nothing else. See `descriptionForm`. **This is the goal of the session, not something the student already knows.** |
| `depends_on` | semicolon-separated `id`s | Which nodes must be mastered first. Empty for root nodes. **This field alone determines the layout**; there is no manual positioning anywhere. |
| `aids` | semicolon-separated level numbers | The assessment context in which mastery is to be demonstrated: `1`, `2` or `1;2`, numbers the tree defines itself in its `aids.*` settings. See `aidsField`. Optional; usually empty. |
| `instruction` | text | Node-specific addition to the AI instruction. **Not the whole instruction** — only what is unique to this node. Usually empty. |

`depends_on` must describe a **directed acyclic graph**. The engine validates this at load time
and names the nodes involved in any cycle it finds.

Several fields can contain commas, so quote them properly. Do not store composed AI instruction
text in the CSV — it is generated.

### The same file also holds the settings

`tree.csv` is the whole tree, not only its nodes. The `type` column says what a row is:

| `type` | The row is | Where its parts go |
|---|---|---|
| `skill` \| `concept` | a node, as above | the columns mean what the table above says |
| `config` | a setting | `name` = the key, `description` = the value |
| `prompt` | a teaching instruction you have rewritten | `topic` = which instruction, `name` = which section, `instruction` = your text |

**A `prompt` row uses published names.** `topic` is the instruction's key: `node` (practice tutor), `exam` (test generator), `motivation` (motivation dialogue) or `lessonPlan` (lesson-plan generator); empty means all four, and a row naming one instruction wins. `name` is the section keyword, listed at **aiskilltrees.com/prompts/** and printed in front of each part of the composed instruction (`tone: …`). Only that section is replaced. Unknown names are reported as errors.

**Put the `config` rows at the top of the file, before the nodes.** The settings a tree needs:

| Key | What it is |
|---|---|
| `schemaVersion` | `3` |
| `title` | What the tree is called |
| `description` | One sentence, shown under the title |
| `language` | The tree's language: `en`, `nb`, `sv`, `de` … |
| `learner` | What the learner is CALLED: `pupil`, `student` or `participant`. Decides the lead-in the panel prints in front of every description, and the word the instructions use. Optional; each language has its own default — school in Norwegian, university in English. The inflected forms live in the language file, so only the key goes here. |
| `subjectFamily` | `mathematics`, `natural-sciences` or `social-sciences` |
| `features.motivation` | `true` to offer the motivation conversation |
| `features.exams` | `true` only if you also supply an `exams.csv` |
| `slots.courseName` | The course as it should be named to a student |
| `slots.motivationSubject` | The subject in one everyday word |
| `slots.expressionFocus` | What students in this subject habitually get sloppy about in how they write |
| `slots.courseSpecifics` | Optional: what is true of THIS course as a whole and should hold in every instruction the tree hands out. Empty by default, and the only setting that reaches all four of them at once |
| `topicOrder` | Optional: the column order, semicolon-separated. Left out, it is worked out from the graph |
| `aids.label`, `aids.<n>.name`, `aids.<n>.student`, `aids.<n>.model` | Optional: the assessment contexts, see `aidsField` |
| `decompositionVersion` | The version of this specification the tree was built against, e.g. `2.7.0`. Shown under "About the course" |

**`slots.courseSpecifics`** is for what is true of the whole course (e.g. the skills are practised on real people, a tool the course forbids must not be suggested). It reaches all four instructions and overrides their defaults, so keep it short. What applies to one node goes in the `instruction` column; a rewrite of one section of one instruction is a `prompt` row.

**An unknown key is an error**, reported with the row number and a guess at what was meant.

### Example rows

```csv
id,type,topic,name,description,depends_on,aids,instruction
,config,,schemaVersion,3,,,
,config,,title,Mathematics 2P,,,
,config,,language,en,,,
,config,,learner,student,,,
,config,,subjectFamily,mathematics,,,
,config,,features.motivation,true,,,
,config,,slots.courseName,mathematics 2P,,,
,config,,slots.motivationSubject,maths,,,
,config,,slots.expressionFocus,"leaves out units, or uses the equals sign to chain steps that are not equal",,,
,config,,decompositionVersion,2.7.0,,,
,config,,aids.label,Part,,,
,config,,aids.1.student,"Without aids: you work by hand, with no calculator.",,,
,config,,aids.1.model,"This is examined in the part of the exam without aids. Expect the student to work by hand, with no calculator.",,,
,config,,aids.2.student,"With aids: you may use a calculator and a spreadsheet.",,,
,config,,aids.2.model,"This is examined in the part of the exam with aids. Expect the student to use a calculator or a spreadsheet for the arithmetic.",,,
,prompt,node,tone,"This row is optional. It replaces one section of the practice tutor.",,,"Be friendly, keep answers short, and do not use emoji."
fraction-decimal,concept,Percentages,Fractions and decimals,"Fraction: a number written as one whole divided into equal parts.
Decimal: the same number written with a decimal point. Every fraction has a decimal form and the reverse.",,,
percentage,concept,Percentages,Percentage,"Percentage: a number of hundredths, so 40 % means 40 out of 100.",fraction-decimal,,
growth-factor,skill,Percentages,Calculate the growth factor from a percentage,calculate the growth factor given a percentage change (increase or decrease).,fraction-decimal;percentage,1;2,"Focus on the bare calculation: given a percentage, find the growth factor. No context or interpretation required."
compare-fraction-decimal,skill,Percentages,Explain the difference between a fraction and a decimal,"explain what the two notations each make easy to see, and say which one a given question is better served by.",fraction-decimal,1,
```
sections.whichConcepts:
The central rule: **a concept earns a node only if something further down the tree breaks when a student does not understand that word in its technical sense.**

Ordinary language gets no node, including everyday words used in a subject context. The technical sense does: "average speed" earns a node, the everyday word "speed" does not. Without this rule the map fills with trivial nodes.

### The threshold depends on the cohort

Whether a load-bearing word gets a node *in this subject* depends on how safely the whole cohort already has it automatic:

1. **Position in the sequence**: the closer to where the word is first taught, the lower the threshold.
2. **Self-selection**: a compulsory subject has a low threshold, so decompose generously. An elective late in a sequence has a high one: a node only for what is genuinely new in this subject.

Example: *coordinate system* is a node in lower-secondary mathematics, a judgement call in a general upper-secondary subject, and not a node in an advanced elective.

### In practice

Go through the competence aims and list which subject terms later nodes depend on. Give each its own concept node, **even if most students already know it**: they simply tick it off quickly, and the map stays honest about what later nodes rest on.
sections.dependencies:
`depends_on` is also the **vocabulary boundary** for the AI instruction: the tutor may use words from a node's prerequisites freely, and must explain any term that first appears in the node itself. A missing dependency lets it pitch explanations above the student.

Check deliberately for the two common failures:

- **Cross-topic dependencies get missed.** A statistics node resting on a fractions node is the typical case, and such links are what make the graph worth more than a list of topics.
- **Unneeded dependencies get added.** A dependency means *cannot be done first*, not *usually taught first*. Prune conventional ordering; it costs the student a false prerequisite.
sections.aidsField:
The `aids` column records the assessment context in which mastery is shown, e.g. the Norwegian maths exam's parts without and with aids, or IB Paper 1 and Paper 2. It belongs to the context, not the skill, and is **optional with no default**: fill it only where it is worth telling the student.

- **The tree defines its own levels** as `config` rows in its own language: `aids.label` is the word before the number ("Part" gives "Part 1"), `aids.<n>.student` is what the student is told the level means, `aids.<n>.model` is what the AI instruction tells the model, and `aids.<n>.name` optionally replaces "Part n". What each level permits is written there and nowhere else.
- **A node names its levels** in the `aids` column, semicolon-separated: `1`, `2`, or `1;2`.
- **A subject without the distinction leaves the column empty and writes no `aids.*` rows.** That switches the field off.
sections.workingWithAnAgent:
The model produces the first draft from the curriculum, or from the teacher's own topic list where the curriculum may not be shared, and the teacher revises it. Curricula differ in copyright status: in Norway and Sweden they are regulations and free to share, while a private examination body's syllabus is its property. Pasting a document into a model is copying, so this is settled before any of it is shared.

The model is reliable at enumerating outcomes, proposing dependencies within a topic, and keeping to the schema. It tends to **make a node for every technical term it meets**, cannot infer the cohort threshold without being told, and **under-generates cross-topic dependencies**; those need the teacher's judgement. Treat a first pass as a draft to cut down, not to extend.
sections.sourceMaterial: **Write every description in your own words. Never copy curriculum text, textbook prose or exam questions into `tree.csv`.** A description is a learning outcome for this tree, level and cohort; pasted text makes worse nodes. If the tree may ever be published, it also matters for licensing: published trees carry an open licence, and textbooks and exam papers are copyrighted almost everywhere. Using such material as background is normal: record in the subject note what was consulted and that no source text or problem numbers were reproduced. Never conceal a source.
sections.checklist:
1. Write the subject note: cohort, position, self-selection and family (`cohort`), and whether the tree is private or for publication (`sourceMaterial`).
2. Read the family block (`subjectFamilies`).
3. List the curriculum's competence aims, checking first what may be shared with a model (`workingWithAnAgent`).
4. Pick the load-bearing concepts against the threshold (`whichConcepts`).
5. Split any concept carrying extensive procedural work into a concept and a skill node (`whatIsANode`).
6. Write `tree.csv` per `dataModel`, `config` rows first. Descriptions follow `descriptionForm`: a bare verb phrase for a skill, `Term: definition` for a concept, and no "the student can" anywhere.
7. Add the dependencies, then a second pass for cross-topic ones (`dependencies`).
8. If the subject distinguishes assessment contexts, write the `aids.*` rows and fill the `aids` column where it matters; if not, leave both out (`aidsField`).
9. Put this specification's version in `decompositionVersion`, and list consulted sources in the subject note.
10. The file is opened at aiskilltrees.com/make-your-own/ to be drawn, checked, and turned into a single HTML file for students.
11. The instructions students get are at aiskilltrees.com/prompts/; rewriting a section is a `prompt` row (`dataModel`).
sections.subjectFamilies: The rules for each family of subjects follow this specification, one block per family, headed by its key. Use the block for the subject in hand and ignore the others; if the family is unclear, ask the teacher. If the blocks are missing, say so and ask for them rather than inventing them.
